sections.sectionText: SP22 ENGL 150:Black Literature in America: The Afterlife of Property. Literary critic Saidiya Hartman writes in her 2008 essay “Venus in Two Acts” that “Wrestling with the [enslaved] girl’s claim on the present is a way of naming our time, thinking our present, and envisioning the past which has created it.” In this survey of African American literature from 1746 to the present, structured by Hartman’s conception of the relationship between the past and the present as “the afterlife of property,” we will read a collection of texts that speak to what it has meant to be a black subject in the United States over the past three centuries. How does history inform the way that African American experiences are transformed into literary expression? What links can we as contemporary readers draw between literature that emerges from past sociocultural and political contexts and our present-day understandings of racial (and gender, sexuality, and class) identity? Beginning with slave narratives and considering fiction, drama, poetry, essay, and contemporary film, we will attempt in this class to understand African American literature as a tradition haunted and informed by the fraught history of black bodies in the Americas, continually speaking to and reaching beyond “property” as legacy and inheritance.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 202 / CWL 253 / MDVL 201 - Medieval Literature and Culture - Carson Koepke - In this course, we will explore the literary and cultural diversity of the Middle Ages by reading and analyzing narratives from Africa, Asia, Europe, and Mesoamerica around the turn of the first millennium. We will experience how medieval peoples thought about physical and metaphysical travel, how they retold epic myths and origin stories, and how the genre of the medieval romance laid the foundations for the modern novel. Readings (in Modern English translation) will be sourced from a wide variety of religious and linguistic traditions, including Old English, Arabic, Coptic, Chinese, Persian, Japanese, Old Norse, and K'iche' Mayan. As we read, we will work to place narratives like "Beowulf" and "The Tale of Genji" within their wider cultural contexts while also thinking critically about what features and practices unite literature across cultures.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 206 / CWL 257 - Enlightenment Literature and Culture - Hina Nazar - Have you ever wondered what people mean when they say that the United States is a child of the Enlightenment, or that the Enlightenment is under attack by nativist forces, or that we need to return to Enlightenment values? This course enables you to engage such statements knowledgeably by providing a broad-based introduction to the Enlightenment, a multifaceted cultural and intellectual development of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (roughly the period 1650-1800). While many of you are probably familiar with key texts and figures of the American Enlightenment, this course focuses on the European—and, more particularly, the British—Enlightenment, which preceded the founding of the United States. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, Europe witnessed unprecedented social, economic, political, and cultural changes that collectively produced a giant leap toward the world we inhabit today. It was an Age of Revolution and of newfound faith in the rights of the individual though these rights were by no means extended to all. It was an Age of Reason, of tremendous advances in science and technology, though reason was by no means the only altar at which so-called enlightened individuals worshipped: God and sentiment remained powerful forces throughout the long eighteenth century. We will consider how the modern mindset that is associated with the Enlightenment was developed by some of the most significant texts of the period, and how it challenged traditional understandings of duty and humanity’s place in the world. Our readings are divided into four modules. After an overview of the Enlightenment spirit in Module 1, we will dig deeper into such crucial concerns of the period as property, race, and empire (Module 2); morality or virtue (Module 3); and education (Module 4). Gender figures prominently in all four modules since women were finding a public voice and entering the literary marketplace in unprecedented numbers at this time. As the moment in history that is credited with creating the modern world, the Enlightenment continues to speak to us today—as is evidenced by its continued currency in public discourse—and our aim this semester is not only to understand its core values but also to link them with our own.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 208 - Victorian Literature and Culture - Eleanor Courtemanche - The Victorian age in Britain (1837-1901) resembles our globalized era in many ways. Like ours, the Victorian age was shaped by a sense of rapid, exhilarating technological progress; a global empire that led to cosmopolitan engagement with other cultures as well as constant military conflict; a hope that free markets were the key to progress; vigorous debate about the role of religion; and women’s ongoing struggle to find a balance between family duties and personal visions. Victorian literature—torn between realism and romance—is an attempt to make sense of all this by balancing material concerns with spiritual needs and the search for beauty. Readings in this interdisciplinary class will include Charlotte Brontë’s “Jane Eyre,” the nostalgic poetry of the Pre-Raphaelites Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Christina Rossetti, Alfred Tennyson’s tragic elegy “In Memoriam,” Olive Schreiner’s novel “The Story of an African Farm,” Oscar Wilde’s play “The Importance of Being Earnest,” political essays by John Stuart Mill and Thomas Carlyle, discussions of Victorian religion and science, and the Crimean War memoir of the Jamaican nurse Mary Seacole. The course will require two short papers, a midterm and final written by hand in person, weekly written assignments, and active class participation. Prerequisite: Completion of the Composition I requirement.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 219 - Literature and Medicine - Andrew Gaedtke - This course introduces students to the literature of medicine. We will take up questions at the forefront of “medical humanities”—an interdisciplinary field that examines cultural ideas about illness and disability, the dramas and power dynamics of the clinic, and the lived experiences of both doctors and patients. We will think through the ways that conceptions of “wellness" are not simply given or universal but are shaped by the literature we read, the advertisements we see, and the stories that are told by doctors and patients. We will ask what kinds of narratives, character types, and assumptions about health and illness can be discerned from literatures of medicine and how have these changed over time. Are there alternative attitudes toward these experiences that we might be able to recognize in new or forgotten representations of health and illness? In what ways have assumptions about race, gender, sexuality, and “the human” been constructed through ideas about health, illness, and disability? How can health care professionals’ delivery of care be improved through forms of literary training and knowledge? The course is open to all and may be of special interest to students who are considering a future in health care. Will discuss fiction, plays, and essays by Virginia Woolf, Charlotte Perkins Gilman, Audre Lorde, Siri Hustvedt, Ian McEwan, Roxane Gay, Susan Sontag, and others.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 241 - Modern Poetry - Tim Newcomb - In 1900 many people seriously believed that poetry as a type of literary writing was so thoroughly obsolete in the modern world that it was about to disappear altogether. Instead, something amazing happened beginning around 1912. Instead of withering away, poetry took off. Within two decades, poets enjoyed more cultural prestige than ever before. Magazines and prizes devoted themselves to “the New Verse.” Writers such as Robert Frost, Carl Sandburg, Edna St. Vincent Millay, and T. S. Eliot were world-famous. They, along with Wallace Stevens, William Carlos Williams, Marianne Moore, and Langston Hughes, wrote some of the greatest poems in the English language. In ENGL 241 we will take an American journey through the poetry written between 1910 and 1950, tracing how that startling reversal of fortune happened when poets rejected Victorian traditions and embraced the styles, subjects, and voices of 20th-century modernity. Grades will be based on a series of short discussion assignments, class participation, multiple analytical essays, and a final examination.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 253 - New Media, Literature, and the Arts - Tess McNulty - Analyzing Content - The internet is awash with new popular cultural forms, from listicles and makeup tutorials to TikToks and AI slop. And yet scholars have only just begun to analyze this new digital “content”: what makes it unique, and how it has been reshaping twenty-first century culture. In this course, we’ll look at new forms of popular digital content in detail, considering them as creative, aesthetic forms of popular entertainment. That might mean reading tweets or YouTube transcripts as closely as if they were poems, or exploring the substance of 100,000 Instagram images. We’ll survey the methods that have been developed, in different disciplines (media theory, art and literary criticism, sociology), for analyzing content in this direct and detailed manner, as well as those that have yet to be attempted. To put theory into practice, students will develop research projects on popular digital artifacts of their choosing. They will also be introduced to computational methods of analyzing content, and have the opportunity to pursue these methods further (though no prior experience with computation is required).

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 255 - Trish Loughran - Survey of Early American Literature and Culture - This is a course that is meant to introduce you to early American literature even as it invites you to theorize the practice of “literary history” and the problems we face in “surveying” large chunks of it at a time, from the disjointed position of the present. To do this, we will explore many classic examples of American literature from some of its earliest iterations up until the crackup we call the Civil War. But we will also sometimes consider the ripples these early works have produced across the timeline of American literature, punctuating our readings of earlier texts with contemporary texts by living American writers who are trying, like us, to make sense of what happened once upon a time, back “then.” Along the way, we will consider a wide variety of materials—from paintings and engravings to novels, poems, letters, and essays. Our goal is to think widely and flexibly about the three words that make up the title of the course: What is a “survey”? What is an “American”? And what is “literature”?

sections.sectionText: GER 251 / ENGL 266 / CWL 254 The Grimms’ Fairy Tales in Context Students read classical and little-known tales from the Grimms' 19th-century collections, as well as earlier tales and other texts, focusing on how power, gender, race, class, and ecological issues play out in these surprisingly dense, meaningful, and very old stories. Why do we continue to tell these tales? Why do certain stories recur again and again, in Western and other cultures? The power of narrative is at the center of our lives, and of these tales, and by the end of the semester we will understand this power much better. This course fulfills General Education requirements in Literature and the Arts, and in Western and Comparative Culture.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL / GWS 280 - African American Women Writers - In this seminar, students examine the ways in which 19th- and 20th-century African American women writers, such as Zora Neale Hurston, Alice Walker, Toni Morrison, and Audre Lorde have articulated notions of womanhood, femininity, and American citizenship through their representations of Black female narrators and characters. The class will begin with Iola Leroy, or Shadows Uplifted by Frances Harper (1892)—one of the first novels published by an African American woman—and end with Sarah Phillips by Andrea Lee (1984). Through this course, we explore the historical marginalization and silencing of Black women’s voices in the American literary canon, not only engaging Black women’s literature, but also literary and cultural studies scholarship by, about, and for Black women. We will interrogate why these women’s voices have been muted and discuss the ways in which their words have been recovered through the hard work of other Black women writers like Alice Walker, who is responsible for the re-emergence of Zora Neale Hurston and her 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. Through weekly reading assignments, lectures, and discussions, this class will culminate in final papers and presentations about one of our course texts.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 325 - Topics in LGBT Literature and Film - Siobhan Somerville - Queer Migrations - This course invites you to explore queer studies approaches to narratives of migration in literature and film. Such migrations can occur between urban and rural spaces, across national borders, across racialized and gendered boundaries and other spaces. We will explore: (1) how migration by LGBTQ people has been represented in fiction, memoir, and film; and (2) how certain migrations might themselves be understood as queer (in the sense of being non-normative). How does migration shape the entangled experiences of sexuality, race, indigeneity, gender, national identity, citizenship, and labor in the texts we study? What aesthetic choices do these authors and filmmakers make in their representation of these varied migrations? In addition to literary texts and films, we will read selected scholarship, not only from the interdisciplinary field of migration studies, but also from perspectives such as queer of color critique, settler colonial studies, transnational feminist theory, and queer indigenous studies.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 350 - Writing about Literature, Text, and Culture - Tony Pollock - Money and Power in Eighteenth-Century Literature - The global economic system we take for granted actually produced heated debate among Anglo-European writers during its emergence in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries: should what we now call capitalism be embraced or rejected, and on what grounds? What’s more, this argument was carried out in literary culture—in journalism and philosophy, of course, but also in plays, novels, and even poems—and it maps onto a gradual shift in attitudes toward two contrasting ideals of masculinity: 1) the libertine, a Restoration figure associated with the indulgence of passions at odds with discipline and moral norms; and 2) the merchant, whose commitment to profitable self-interest promised to enhance the social good as well. In addition to considering these issues, the writers we will study also think intensely about how women are supposed to position themselves in the new economic order: what social identities and forms of agency could women pursue (or not) in the “age of commerce,” with what affordances and what risks? As heavy as these themes may sound, our reading will focus significantly on satirical poems by Rochester, Mandeville, and Swift; theatrical comedies by Wycherley and Behn; and an “anti-novel” by Eliza Haywood, mocking the era’s most popular work of fiction.

restrictions: Restricted to English or Creative Writing or Creative Writing major(s) or minor(s).
sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 350 - Writing about Literature, Text, and Culture - Manisha Basu - The Politics of Motherhood - The Politics of Motherhood emerges from a serious concern with the war being waged on reproductive justice in a global political context increasingly dominated by the Religious Right. The term ‘reproductive justice’ combines discourses of reproductive rights and social justice, and so it is as much a pathway into thinking through human rights as it is about centering a woman’s sovereignty over her body. To approach this topic, we will assume a transnational and deeply historical approach, trying to understand how motherhood was tied in seventeenth and eighteenth-century Europe to technologies of nation formation and empire-building, how it became a violently contested site in the course of the Atlantic Slave Trade, how it has torn apart Indigenous and Black communities, particularly in the Americas where the state, in an allegedly benevolent parental guise, took children away from their families, and how it has functioned as the grounds on which the battle for food sovereignty and food justice comes to light. We will read through novels, critical works, short stories, fairy tales, and poems from across the world – Zimbabwe, Ghana, the Caribbean, India, the Americas, and Europe – to grapple with motherhood as a political issue and a culturally specific function that belies its more traditional understanding as a universally idealized expectation largely tied to woman’s care-giving positionality.

restrictions: Restricted to English or Creative Writing or Creative Writing major(s) or minor(s).
sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 350 - Writing About Literature, Text, and Culture - Barry Hudek - Willa Cather: Immigration and Americanization - NYT columnist Bret Stephens believes that Cather’s work provides the “perfect antidote” to hateful rhetoric regarding today’s immigration debate. Our class will examine Stephens’ claim, comparing and contrasting today’s climate with that of Cather’s late 19th and early 20th century settings depicted in her novels and short stories. Several small essays and responses will lead to a traditional, capstone research essay.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL/MACS 373 - Special Topics in Film Studies - Tim Newcomb - Citizens Coen: The Cinema of the Coen Brothers - Over the past forty years Ethan and Joel Coen have occupied a unique place in American cinematic culture, as auteurs of a postmodern cinema that gleefully violates the stylistic “rules of the game” while also paying homage to previous moments in American films. Their films consistently foreground their own roles as creators, which has made them key predecessors for later “star” directors such as Quentin Tarantino and Spike Jonze; yet in their personal lives they avoid celebrity, remaining intensely devoted to their distinctive artistic vision. They have won many awards including Oscars, but are still regarded with skepticism by some critics who find their films all about style and genre pastiche. This class will explore these contradictions and many others as we survey their major films, as well as one of the “originals” that inspired them to rethink cinematic genres, especially the screwball comedy, the Hitchcockian thriller, the gangster picture, the western, and the hard-boiled film noir. Most of the Coens’ films will be examined, including Blood Simple, Raising Arizona, Miller’s Crossing, Barton Fink, Fargo, O Brother Where Art Thou?, No Country for Old Men, Hail Caesar!, and of course, The Big Lebowski. The course features a mandatory weekly in-class screening and a 2-hour weekly discussion session. Grades will be based on class participation, multiple analytical essays and a final exam.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 380 - Topics in Writing Studies - John Gallagher - Influencer Cultures - Social media has pervaded society through the language of content and influencers. In this course, we examine 21st century media theory as it relates to online discourse of creator cultures. Together, then, we’ll analyze how users build communities, tell stories, and push back against algorithms. These stories will help us study influencer culture, fandoms, content moderation, or viral trends. Consequently, students will gain practical research experience, receive one-on-one mentoring, and sharpen our academic and professional writing skills. No AI tool can compete with the research or writing students will produce in this class.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 396 - English Honors Seminar - Bob Markley - Lit and Culture of the Vietnam Era - This course will focus on the literature and culture of the Vietnam War in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s. This conflict, which ended a half century ago, remains a crucial force in American literary and political culture. We will read novels by Vietnamese and Vietnamese-American authors, including Duong Thu Huong (Novel without a Name), Bao Ninh (The Sorrow of War), and Viet Thanh Nguyen, (The Sympathizer), as well as works by American writers who served in Vietnam, including Tim O’Brien (The Things They Carried) and Michael Herr (Dispatches). Also, we will explore some of the refractions of this era in popular music (Arlo Guthrie, Bob Dylan, Jimmy Hendrix, and Joan Baez, among others) and film (Full Metal Jacket, Apocalypse Now). During the semester, you will learn about the draft, anti-war protests, the Civil Rights movement, feminism, and the complicated politics of the era. Because this is a class about war in Southeast Asia and protests in the United States, please be advised that the readings will include accounts—often graphic accounts--of battlefield violence, sexual violence, racism, drug and alcohol addiction, and suicide. That said, we will explore what individuals and groups of people learned from the Vietnam era, how the legacy of the war has shaped responses to conflicts in the 21st century, and how anti-war protests have continued to shape progressive movements in Vietnam as well as the US. Students will be responsible for short oral presentations, an oral exam at the end of the semester; in-class writing assignments, and a final project that does not use AI.

SP27 ENGL 396 - English Honors Seminar - Candice Jenkins - Black Horror - Since the dramatic success of Jordan Peele’s 2017 blockbuster film, Get Out, Black horror has become ubiquitous in popular culture, particularly in contemporary film and television. But this genre has a much longer history in American and African American literature and culture, and as Robin R. R. Means Coleman has argued, there’s an important distinction to be made between mainstream horror that includes African American characters, and “Black horror,” which centers Black subjects’ fears and anxieties, often including anti-Blackness. In this honors seminar, we will consider what makes a horror story “Black,” and what Black horror has to say about both Blackness and American culture. We will study fiction and film by Ryan Coogler, Nia DaCosta, Tananarive Due, Victor LaValle, Toni Morrison, Jordan Peele, Rivers Solomon, Jesmyn Ward, and Kai Ashante Wilson, among others. Attendance and active participation, group podcast, in-class writing, final paper.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 418 - Shakespeare - Lori Newcomb - In Shakespeare’s lifetime (1564-1616), professional drama was a new form of entertainment in a new kind of venue, the commercial stage. Like many of today’s entertainment forms, plays were products of collaboration among playwrights, actors, and audiences. The plays, written as scripts for performance, were popular culture: first performed live, only later published for readers, and much later reimagined as ‘literature.” Today, the plays live on as entertainment, heritage, and challenge, allowing users to engage with recurring human dreams and nightmares, with harmony and tyranny, with disorder and with reconciliation. The original texts’ language and stage action leaves unusual leeway for variation and reimagining by later interpreters. Societies in turmoil continue to find the plays powerful tools for communicating about difficult issues, thinking through historical change, and imagining alternatives to the status quo. We’ll read 6 or 7 plays in depth, enjoying their daring explorations of the period’s family, political, gender/sexual, religious and racial tensions. Our learning will be active and embodied whenever possible. Thus, to consider the plays as performance texts, we’ll get on our feet and stage a few scenes. We’ll explore the ambiguities of the written script, and the printed playbook as itself a new technology. We’ll support historicist and feminist, queer-studies, and anti-racist perspectives by drawing on key nonfiction texts of the day. Beyond the classroom, you’ll visit the Rare Book Library, make your own ‘playbook,’ and write an academic analysis of a live theater production. Other written work includes in-class writings focused on short passages, a longer paper with guided research (8-10 pp.), and a final exam. Primary textbook: Norton Shakespeare: Essential Plays and Sonnets, 3rd edition, print edition required. I’ll provide contextual and critical readings.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 427 - Eighteenth-Century Literature - Hina Nazar - Gender and Enlightenment - This course offers an introduction to some of the most significant works of British literature in the long eighteenth century (1660-1800) by homing in on the period’s fascination with gender distinctions, and, more particularly, the question of women’s rights, capabilities, virtue, and sexuality. What became known in later times as “the woman question” was hotly debated in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Britain owing to new understandings of natural rights and scientific inquiry, and new claims about the potential of rational individuals to challenge the authority of the church and state. And yet, in this Age of Reason or Age of Enlightenment, the dominant cultural conception of women was that they were creatures of unreason, or flighty descendant of the first woman, Eve, who brought misery upon all mankind. Our course considers how male and female writers of the period—poets, dramatists, novelists, as well as political philosophers, feminist pamphleteers, and writers of conduct and religious manuals—both reinforced and challenged these stereotypes about women. It also examines how the category of gender interacted with class, race, and empire, as Britain acquired dominance in the transatlantic slave trade and expanded its territorial ambitions. Several of the readings for the course will be short selections from longer works, so that you can cultivate the skill of close reading while learning to situate literary texts in a broader historical context. Authors to be covered include Margaret Cavendish, Katherine Philips, Mary Astell, Alexander Pope, Aphra Behn, Eliza Haywood, Samuel Richardson, Henry Mackenzie, Olaudah Equiano, and Mary Wollstonecraft.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 442 - Contemporary British and Irish Literature - Andrew Gaedtke - Returns of the Repressed in Contemporary British and Irish Literature - This course will consider how unresolved problems of the past continue to haunt contemporary British and Irish literature. These “Returns of the Repressed” may range from personal traumas and difficult truths that have not been fully processed to groups of people who have suffered systematic violence and inequality. The semester will be divided into sections devoted to these returns including past national failures, the aftermath of the global British empire and its collapse, Britain’s treatment of immigrants and postcolonial subjects, the “Troubles” in Northern Ireland, persistent gender inequality and sexual trauma, and questions about the novel’s continued relevance. Some of the texts we will discuss respond to Brexit—the United Kingdom’s exit from the European Union—a political decision that has deeply divided the nation. With recent works of fiction as our guides, we will ask what led to this controversial decision and how the meaning of “British” has been contested. We will ask how innovations in contemporary British literature enable us to rethink larger questions about nationality, trauma, historical responsibility, and their narration. Readings will include works by Anna Burns, Kazuo Ishiguro, Ian McEwan, Guy Gunaratne, Ali Smith, and Zadie Smith.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 455 - Major Authors - Robert Barrett - Terry Pratchett's Discworld - The British writer Terry Pratchett is best known for his Discworld series, forty-one novels published between 1983 and 2015 and set on Discworld, a flat planet transported through interstellar space on the backs of four elephants standing on the shell of the world turtle Great A’Tuin. In these books, Pratchett uses witty (and often groanworthy) wordplay to lampoon not only the clichés of the fantasy genre but also the pretensions and injustices of modern life on Roundworld (his name for the Earth). To get a handle on Pratchett’s use of satire and parody, we’ll begin by reading his Wyrd Sisters in conjunction with its intertext, Shakespeare’s Macbeth. We’ll then make our way through seven more novels from the series: Reaper Man, Small Gods, Men at Arms, Carpe Jugulum, The Fifth Elephant, A Hat Full of Sky, and Going Postal. There will be two exams (a midterm and a final), and the writing assignments for the class will include a few short papers and a longer research project and presentation on one of the thirty-three Discworld books not on the course reading list (no duplications as I want the class to get the broadest possible sense of Pratchett’s work).

restrictions: Not intended for students with Freshman class standing.

SP27 ENGL 455 - Major Authors - Trish Loughran - Marx, Freud, Nietzsche - We could call this course: Marx, Freud, Nietzsche, and Company because we will be reading our three core theorists through a lens provided by two of their most famous readers: Paul Ricouer and Michel Foucault, who, in the 1960s, first identified this trio as the “masters of suspicion,” three major thinkers who invented a new kind of interpretation, a new way of “reading” the world around them that was, more than anything else, committed to unmasking the “illusions of consciousness” in favor of some better, realer truth. We will use this lens to learn more about the lives and theories of MFN (reading widely from their classic texts) and then also ask: what happens next? There’s no doubt that the nineteenth century invented this mode of interpretation and that the twentieth century embraced it. But is it still the best way to read, think, and theorize in the 21C? That is the question we will work towards. Note that this is a course primarily designed for theory-curious undergraduates who would like the time to read more widely in the work of these core three nineteenth-century thinkers and to find a space to talk to each other about them.

SP27 ENGL 455 - Major Authors - Kim Mack - Ralph Ellison - The profound and enduring impact of Ralph Ellison’s fiction and non-fiction on American arts and letters cannot be overstated. Not only did Ellison win the 1953 National Book Award for Fiction for his novel Invisible Man—the first African American to do so—but he also made his mark as a formidable essayist with his 1964 essay collection, Shadow and Act. This course will explore Ellison’s iconic, award-winning novel; his essays focused on race, American history, and all manner of American culture, including music and literature; and selected letters between himself and other American writers such as Albert Murray, Richard Wright, Saul Bellow, and Kenneth Burke. We will also explore the music (jazz and blues, in particular) that inspired Ellison’s fiction and non-fiction alike. Through weekly reading assignments, lectures, and discussions, this class will culminate in final papers and presentations about one or more of our course texts.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 460 - Literature of American Minorities - Chris Freeburg - Civil Rights and Literature - So many of our great works of national literature emerged around the language, images, and history of the Civil Rights movement in the US. This course studies the literature, poetry, and drama from the middle of the twentieth century that wrestles with the promise of America. We’ll focus on William Faulkner, James Baldwin, Lorraine Hansberry, Carson McCullers, Langston Hughes, and others with a scholarly eye toward the relationship between history, literary art forms, and American politics. In addition to this important literary history, this course will also expose students to important scholarly research. There will be weekly response papers that build into a substantial research paper.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 475 - Literature and Other Disciplines - Lori Newcomb - Book History - This course works at the intersection between literary study and the newer discipline of “the history of the book,” itself a hybrid practice attending to textualities, technologies and readerships. Literary scholars use varied methods to address perennial questions: what is a text? How does it make meaning? Why do we value it as literature? Book historians ask related questions with special attention to material texts: how did books develop? How does the form of a book – its size, its heft, its craft—lend meaning to the text it conveys? Why have we valued books, and how will we continue to do so in an increasingly digital environment? In early modern Britain, about 1550-1750, while writers still composed literary works with quill and ink, the printed book emerged as the dominant vehicle of literary experience. Print publication inevitably reshaped early modern imaginative texts, yet we can still recognize them as profoundly intermedial. Book history gives us many ways to trace the histories of books, from the hands-on to the speculative: learning how to set type for the hand press; poring over rare books to deduce their production process; charting new roles for authors, publishers, and editors; gathering evidence of readership from individual copies as well as critical responses of the period; considering whether the rise of print was itself an agent of social change; and appreciating books’ unique affordances in our digital age. We’ll bring these methods to a core set of early modern texts, including lyric poems, political polemics, stage drama, and pioneering works of prose fiction. We’ll see that texts written by individual men and women, and often enjoyed in direct social exchange or performance, were then packaged for the press in ways that reshaped later readings. Each student will write their own “history” of a short early modern text, where possible in the form of a book from our Rare Book Library, exploring its materiality, its later reception, and/or a future-facing remediation. Readings may include: Michelle Levy and Tom Mole, Broadview Introduction to Book History; Sarah Werner, Studying Early Printed Books, 1450-1800; William Shakespeare, sonnets, Hamlet, and Julius Caesar; Margaret Cavendish, The Blazing World; Charlotte Lennox, The Female Quixote.

This final product will showcase students’ professional development as well-informed writers on environmental issues, and may be published in Q Magazine.

subject: ENGL

info: Same as CWL 503 and MACS 503. See MACS 503.

sections.sectionText: While the title of this course is "Historiography of Cinema," it is designed to incorporate issues of moving image culture more broadly. Cinema studies provides the longest and most thorough discourse on moving image culture, and therefore this course introduces methodology and theory beneficial to students working on topics in television, video art, advertising, and digital media-making, and more. The aim of this class is to introduce and train students in research methods and approaches in moving image studies, and discuss how the long tradition of cinematic scholarly discourse can impact research in other areas of media and various periods of technological emergence. Each class session includes a screening (usually about 90 min) of a film appropriate to the following week's reading.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL / MDVL 514 - Seminar in Medieval Literature - Carson Koepke - Reconstructing Old English in the Long Seventeenth Century - This iteration of ENGL 514 is an Old English reception course based in the antiquarian, religious, and philological scholarship of the late sixteenth century through the early eighteenth, from Archbishop Matthew Parker and Franciscus Junius to George Hickes and the Elstob siblings. We will read from the first printings of Old English literature and examine these editions and their paratexts through multiple sessions at the RBML. In a sense, we will attempt to recreate the earliest post-medieval environments for scholars and students to learn Old English and read its literature, and we will interrogate their methods by critically engaging with the works they left behind. Topics of study will include the use of early medieval England's literary output as historical evidence for an independent English Church, the (mis)interpretation of Old English as a daughter of the Gothic language, and the mining of primary sources to reconstruct England's political and legal history prior to the Norman Conquest.

subject: ENGL

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 537 - Seminar in Victorian Literature - Eleanor Courtemanche - Victorian Literature and Economic Crisis - Because the industrial revolution started in Britain in the late 18th century, British society was the first in the world to encounter the particular forms of social turmoil that would soon spread to other European societies, and then transform traditional societies around the world. Before the rise of later industrial boom cities like Chicago, the new city of Manchester was considered the cradle of a terrifying future. This graduate seminar will focus on the “industrial novels” that responded to this crisis, as well as the economic theory (both orthodox and heterodox) that attempted to make sense of it. British realist fiction often sought sentimental resolutions to political problems, but also angrily represented the suffering that fueled the riches of the new capitalists. Readings will include Harriet Martineau’s Weal and Woe in Garveloch, Charles Dickens’s Oliver Twist and Hard Times, Elizabeth Gaskell’s Mary Barton and North and South, William Morris’s News from Nowhere, George Bernard Shaw’s Mrs. Warren’s Profession, and Francis Spufford’s Red Plenty, as well as political economy by Adam Smith and Thomas Malthus. We will analyze The Communist Manifesto by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, as well as Engels’s The Condition of the Working Class in England in 1844, and Volume 1 of Marx’s Capital. Theoretical readings will include work by Sven Beckert, Raymond Williams, Jennifer MacLure, Regenia Gagnier, and Thomas Piketty.

subject: ENGL
title: Seminar Afro-American Lit
info: May be repeated if topics vary. Prerequisite: One college course devoted entirely to an aspect of American literature or consent of instructor.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 559 - Seminar in African-American Literature - Chris Freeburg - This course examines seminal works of American literature from writers such as Herman Melville, Mark Twain, William Faulkner, W.E.B. Du Bois, Carson McCullers, and Zora Neale Hurston. The course takes up how these classic writers use Black characters to probe existential questions about what it means to be human and how making characters might be altogether different from thinking 'the human.' To wrestle with this question this course will study the connections between images of Blacks in popular films, music, and print media, and how each writers deepens, complicates, accepts, and/or rejects them. To analyze Black characters in American culture this course will take full advantage of the philosophical writings of Stanley Cavell, Jonathan Lear, Soren Kierkegaard, and Hannah Arendt, recent historical scholarship in Black studies, as well as primary texts from each writer's context. There will be response papers, a presentation, and a substantial research paper.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 582 - Topics in Research and Writing - Melissa Littlefield - Data Feminism - In this course we’ll reconsider the metaphors and material realities of data; explore digital environments such as gaming platforms and internet collectives; and reimagine public, private, and domestic spheres via algorithmic logics. We’ll be paying particular attention to marginalized voices and the methodologies of interdisciplinary fields. Central questions include: what affordances do digital spaces and technologies provide for individuals and groups? What are the limitations, scripts, and gatekeeping mechanisms of these spaces and tools? Who has the power to define key terms, algorithms, and user interfaces? How have feminist, queer, and intersectional concerns influenced and/or challenged each of these questions and issues? This graduate course is intended to serve students in a wide range of disciplines, from the humanities and the social sciences to the sciences—all are welcome! No previous experience with big data, science & technology, or feminist theory is expected or required. This course meets in person, but we may occasionally also “meet” in other virtual environments throughout the semester (via Zoom or otherwise, depending on student projects, presentations, and interests).

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 583 - Topics in Written Pedagogy and Design - Charlesia McKinney - Queer Pedagogies - Centering embodied and affective literacies, we will study uses of the erotic to stimulate queer approaches to teaching and un/learning across public and private pedagogical spheres. While this course prioritizes Writing Studies scholarship, we will also integrate work from related fields.

Prerequisite: Graduate standing in the Department of English or consent of instructor. Students needing the proseminar for their programs will be given priority enrollment.

sections.sectionText: SP27 ENGL 593 - Proseminar in Literature - Andrea Stevens - The Teaching of Literature - This graduate seminar is designed to prepare students from a wide variety of backgrounds to teach literature at the undergraduate level. Although our discussions will be framed by some readings in pedagogical theory (and other, topically relevant articles) chosen by the students, our emphasis will be on the practical: how to develop effective syllabi; how to teach a variety of genres, namely poetry, drama, fiction, and film; how to lead a discussion; how to manage classrooms; how to foster diversity in the classroom; how to recover from the teaching missteps all of us will make. Together, we will 1) analyze the comparative strengths of different pedagogical strategies in achieving a wide range of curricular goals in the literature classroom; 2) develop persuasive and powerful ways of describing precisely what we do as teachers in the humanities, as well as why and how we do it; 3) articulate flexible criteria for designing effective syllabi and assignments for different courses; 4) practice teaching in front of one another; 5) and, by the end of the semester, generate a teaching portfolio suitable for use on the academic job market or for fellowships. We will also go over department, LAS, and campus requirements for core and general education courses. This class is restricted to graduate students from English (CW, Writing Studies, and Literature); interested students from departments outside of English need to receive written permission from the instructor to enroll.
